authority.meaning: Modifies a Golden Rule for a person with a second condition. It may tighten a rule; it may never relax one.
authority.proposed_by: developer, from the sheet's own 'Rationale for Precedence' column and the workflow.html authority order; the client has not confirmed it

enforcement: none: reference only. Modifiers with no number are never enforced, and none is shown to a person as advice.

direction_values.tighten: a lower or stricter limit than the baseline
direction_values.review: the baseline may not apply as it stands; refer to the doctor
direction_values.reverse: the direction itself flips (a target to meet becomes a limit)
direction_values.redirect: the amount stays; the choice of food within the category changes
direction_values.no_exception: a condition that does not unlock any exception to the baseline

rules: A modifier may tighten a Golden Rule; it may never relax one.
When two conditions pull in different directions, the stricter rule applies, and a 'reverse' beats the baseline (CKD and protein).
If no modifier covers the person's combination of conditions, the answer is 'ask your doctor or Dixit coach', never a guess.
A modifier with no number is information only; the recipe gate does not enforce it.
These are general information, not protocol advice for the other condition (KB policy GRC-NEW-21: other conditions go to the person's doctor).

baseline.summary: People with diabetes generally have no special sodium limit beyond the standard advice (added salt under about 2 g a day). Salt does not directly affect blood sugar.

modifiers.summary: Sodium usually needs to run lower than the standard advice; it is one of the more direct diet levers for blood pressure.
Kidney function also affects how the body handles sodium, so the standard limit may not apply as it stands.

precedence.rationale: Hypertension and CKD, not diabetes status, decide the sodium rule; a diabetes-only view would leave out the caveat for someone with both.

kb_text.baseline: People with diabetes generally have no special sodium restriction beyond standard daily guidance (added salt under ~2g/day, DIET-108) — salt does not directly affect blood sugar.
kb_text.modifiers: If hypertension is also present, sodium intake typically needs to run lower than the standard guidance — this is one of the more directly diet-linked levers for blood pressure. If CKD is also present, kidney function affects sodium handling too, another reason the standard limit may not apply as-is.
kb_text.why: Hypertension/CKD are the primary gate for sodium, not diabetes status — a diabetes-only framing would omit the relevant caveat for a comorbid user.

open_questions.text: No number is given for the lower limit in hypertension or CKD, so nothing can be enforced.
'Added salt under about 2 g a day': is that salt or sodium? 2 g of sodium is about 5 g of salt, and the recipe gate counts sodium_mg.
Heart failure is not covered here, although the book and the Condition Context sheet mention a salt-restricted diet for it.

baseline.summary: The general target is about 0.83 g per kg of body weight a day: a floor to meet, not something most people need to limit.

modifiers.summary: Protein may need to be limited instead of met or exceeded, because the kidneys process protein's waste products.
Purine-rich proteins (red meat, seafood) are worth moderating. This is about which protein, not how much.

precedence.rationale: CKD is the one case where the direction itself reverses; hyperuricemia changes the choice of food inside the protein group, not the total.

kb_text.baseline: General target ~0.83 g/kg body weight/day (GRC-031) — a floor to meet, not something most people need to actively limit.
kb_text.modifiers: CKD reverses this: protein may need to be limited rather than met or exceeded, since the kidneys process protein's waste byproducts (DIET-117). Hyperuricemia: purine-rich protein sources specifically (red meat, seafood) are worth moderating — this is about which protein, not how much (DIET-114).
kb_text.why: CKD is the one case where the direction itself reverses, not just the amount — the sharpest test of the baseline+modifier structure. Hyperuricemia modifies food choice within the protein category, not the total.
kb_text.status: Ready — CKD modifier flagged as priority given direct conflict with GRC-031 framing

open_questions.text: The recipe limits table has only a daily_max. This topic needs a floor and a cap, and the cap for CKD has no number.
The Healthful Diet book says 0.75 g/kg (pp. 42, 82). GRC-031 says 0.83 g/kg and was not supplied; the KB figure is used here.
CKD is not split by stage or by dialysis. Dialysis patients are usually advised more protein, not less, so a doctor must confirm this rule.
Plant purines (the book names horse gram and chana dal for vegetarians) are not covered under hyperuricemia.

baseline.summary: Rotate between two unrefined oils, changing weekly when heating. No single oil is presented as necessary or better.

modifiers.summary: Saturated fat (ghee, coconut oil, butter, fatty red meat) is one of the more direct diet levers, so moderation matters more than without a lipid concern.

precedence.rationale: Dyslipidemia is the main gate for moderating saturated fat; the general oil-rotation advice applies to everyone.

topics.kb_status: Ready: sourced, no open conflict. Oil guidance for CKD and heart disease is not covered: an open gap, not guessed.
